A little reflection: I have spent over 25 years working across development, from labor and livelihoods to energy transitions, climate, and sustainable development. I started at the UN as an intern, learning how many roadmaps exist within the system, all aiming toward one goal: creating real impact for people and communities. 

Why am I sharing this? Because when I began my career, my generation aimed to create an impact for communities on the ground. As my work expands, it is often the moments with the next generation of leaders that remind me why I chose this path in the first place. 

To close out a great week of consultations across Bosnia and Herzegovina, I met with students at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and Economics in the University of Sarajevo to discuss something central to the country’s future: the link between energy, digitalization, and opportunity. 

For Bosnia and Herzegovina, the opportunity is real. More than 2,000 MW of new renewable capacity is planned by 2030, yet youth outmigration remains one of the biggest risks. Around 270,000 young people are considering leaving, nearly half of the youth surveyed. Amid these realities, the green economy is creating entirely new demand for engineers, innovators, and problem-solvers.

We spoke about how the clean energy transition is no longer only about producing power, but about designing systems around constraints: smarter grids, storage, AI-driven planning, and local industries that create value and jobs. And as engineers themselves, they are entering the workforce at a moment where they can help define the systems that will shape it. 

Because the future of the transition will depend on whether young people see that they can build that future here.
